chapter.title: How to Contribute to Open Source
chapter.prerequisites: Chapters 1 and 2. No Git or open-source experience needed; a free GitHub account is enough for the lab.
chapter.handsOn: submit a real pull request to robOSStics by fixing a typo, updating an outdated reference, or correcting a broken link using GitHub in the browser or locally.
chapter.summary: Open-source software licenses, public collaboration norms, repository structure, beginner issue discovery, robotics project governance across ROS 2, MoveIt 2, ros2_control, Gazebo, and Nav2, and a hands-on pull request lab.

lessons.title: What Open Source Is
objectives: Explain why an open source license is required for a project to be open source.
Describe how public open-source contributions build experience, reputation, and career artifacts.
Identify standard project files (README, CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, LICENSE) and what each does.
Examine how ROS 2 packages document purpose, build instructions, and permissive licensing.

lessons.title: Your First Contribution
objectives: Identify non-code contributions, including documentation, issue organization, and peer review.
Find beginner-friendly tasks using labels like first-timers-only, good first issue, and help wanted.
Follow the fork, clone, upstream remote, feature branch, and pull request workflow on GitHub.
Apply open-source communication norms: keeping discussions public, providing reproduction steps, and commenting on issues before starting.

lessons.title: How Robotics Projects Work
objectives: Explain the ROS 2 development flow: rolling development, distribution branches, and backport rules.
Satisfy contributor governance requirements, including Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) sign-off and maintainer approvals.
Describe the role of the ROS 2 build farm and REP 2004 quality categories in software stability.
Compare contribution policies across MoveIt 2, ros2_control, Gazebo, and Nav2.

lessons.title: Lab: Your First Pull Request
objectives: Select a small, actionable improvement such as a typo fix, wording clarification, or source correction.
Edit files and open a pull request directly in the web browser using GitHub's file editor.
Clone the repository locally, apply changes, and run the project verification checks before submitting.
Submit a pull request using the repository template and respond constructively to maintainer review.

blurbs.3-1: What open source is: licenses, public artifacts, core repository files (README, CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, LICENSE), and ROS 2 package examples.
blurbs.3-2: Finding your first contribution: non-code tasks, beginner labels, the fork and pull request workflow, and public communication norms.
blurbs.3-3: How robotics projects work: ROS 2 rolling development, backport rules, DCO sign-off, build farm testing, and governance across MoveIt 2, ros2_control, Gazebo, and Nav2.
blurbs.3-4: Lab: making your first pull request to robOSStics by fixing a typo or broken source in the browser or locally with verification checks.

glossary.Apache 2.0 license: A permissive open source license typically required for ROS 2 packages and governing contributions submitted to ros2_control.
glossary.backport: The practice of copying features or bug fixes to older released distributions only after they have been accepted and merged into rolling.
glossary.build farm: The automated build and testing infrastructure at ci.ros2.org running nightly jobs across platforms and architectures.
glossary.CODE_OF_CONDUCT: A document that establishes ground rules for participant behavior to facilitate a friendly, welcoming environment across a project.
glossary.CONTRIBUTING: A project document that helps people contribute by explaining what types of contributions are needed and how the development process works.
glossary.Developer Certificate of Origin: A certification enforced on pull requests requiring commit messages to include a Signed-off-by line confirming the submission's origin.
glossary.draft pull request: A pull request opened early or marked WIP to get early feedback from reviewers before the work is finished.
glossary.first-timers-only: An issue label that explicitly marks issues that are easier than normal and reserved exclusively for newcomers who have never contributed to open source before.
glossary.force-push: A git push operation that overwrites remote history, prohibited after a PR has been reviewed because it breaks the GitHub review UI.
glossary.fork: A personal copy of an open source repository on GitHub that allows a contributor to create edit branches.
glossary.good first issue: An issue label used by ROS 2 and MoveIt to designate approachable tasks for first-time contributors.
glossary.help wanted: An issue label applied in Gazebo and ROS 2 to broader tasks that maintainers think should be tackled by the community.
glossary.open source license: A legal grant that every open source project must have, without which a project is not open source.
glossary.pull request: A proposed contribution submitted from a branch to an upstream repository for review and merging.
glossary.README: An instruction manual that welcomes community members, explains why the project is useful, and provides getting started instructions, descriptions, and usage examples.
glossary.REP 2004: A ROS Enhancement Proposal defining quality categories that establish differentiated standards for package versioning, testing, and documentation.
glossary.rolling: The active ROS 2 development branch where features and fixes must be accepted and merged before backporting to older releases.
glossary.Squash and Merge: A merge method used for approved pull requests to consolidate commits and keep a clean history before deleting the branch.
glossary.trivial change: A minor pull request change such as whitespace removal or typo correction that does not require DCO sign-off in ROS 2.
glossary.upstream: The original repository remote from which a fork is cloned, pulled regularly to keep local code updated and reduce merge conflicts.
glossary.pull request template: A file in a repository that pre-fills every new pull request with prompts and a checklist, so contributors give reviewers the information they need.
glossary.Propose changes: The step in GitHub's web editor where you describe your edit before it becomes a pull request.
glossary.generated regions: Parts of this site's files that scripts/site_sync.py builds automatically, such as the sitemap, hub rows and navigation bars; they are not edited by hand.

quiz.question: According to open source definitions, what is required for a project to be open source?
choices: An open source license
At least two independent maintainers
Hosting on a public git forge
A dedicated community discussion forum
quiz.explanation: Every open source project must have an open source license, and without an open source license a project is not open source.

quiz.question: Which license is typically required in the LICENSE file of every ROS 2 package?
choices: GNU General Public License v3
Apache 2.0 license
Mozilla Public License 2.0
Creative Commons Attribution 4.0
quiz.explanation: Every ROS 2 package must have a LICENSE file, typically the Apache 2.0 license unless an existing permissive license is in place.

quiz.question: According to the study by Igor Steinmacher, what share of casual contributions to open source consists of documentation?
quiz.explanation: A study by Igor Steinmacher found that 28% of casual contributions to open source are documentation, such as typo fixes, reformatting, or writing a translation.

quiz.question: How does the first-timers-only label distinguish open source issues?
choices: They carry financial bounties funded by project sponsors
They require an architecture review before any branch is created
They are easier than normal and reserved exclusively for newcomers who have never contributed to open source before
They are restricted to non-code documentation changes
quiz.explanation: The first-timers-only label explicitly marks issues that are easier than normal and reserved exclusively for newcomers who have never contributed to open source before.

quiz.question: What is prohibited within an already released ROS distribution?
choices: Nightly automated testing on the build farm
Documentation corrections and typo fixes
Major version increments and breaking API changes
Backporting bug fixes accepted in rolling
quiz.explanation: Major version increments and breaking API changes are prohibited within an already released ROS distribution.

quiz.question: In ROS 2 development, where must a feature or fix be accepted and merged before opening a backport pull request to older releases?
choices: The rolling branch
The humble distribution branch
A private fork repository
The ros2_documentation repository
quiz.explanation: In ROS 2 development, features or fixes must be accepted and merged into the rolling branch before opening a pull request to backport them to older releases.

quiz.question: When is Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) sign-off exempt on a ROS 2 pull request?
choices: When submitted by external contributors without repository write permissions
When the pull request only performs trivial changes such as whitespace removal or typo corrections
When modifying Python scripts instead of C++ source files
When the pull request has passed all build farm tests
quiz.explanation: DCO sign-off in ROS 2 is not required for pull requests that only perform trivial changes such as whitespace removal or typo corrections.

quiz.question: Why does the ros2_control project prohibit force-pushing to a pull request branch after review has taken place?
choices: It deletes test logs from the automated build farm
It breaks the GitHub review UI
It voids the project's Apache 2.0 license
It triggers an automatic branch deletion
quiz.explanation: In ros2_control, contributors must not force-push after a PR has been reviewed because force-pushing breaks the GitHub review UI.

quiz.question: When you edit a robOSStics lesson in the GitHub web editor, what do you do after writing a short title and summary of your change?
choices: Run the four checks locally
Click Propose changes, then Create pull request
Email the maintainer
Push directly to main
quiz.explanation: CONTRIBUTING.md: write a short title and a one-sentence summary, then click Propose changes and Create pull request.

quiz.question: You want to suggest a new source but have never used scripts/sources.py. What does CONTRIBUTING.md say?
choices: You cannot contribute until you learn the script
Open an issue or pull request with the suggested source URL; maintainers check it and update docs/sources.json
Edit sitemap.xml by hand
Add the source without a citation
quiz.explanation: Maintainers check the claims, run the script and update docs/sources.json for you.
